Everyone and Everything in Dad's Care This Week, on One Page

The people, phone numbers, notes and dates you already have, and a list of what's missing.

Download PDF

The nurse's name is in a voicemail, the appointment is in your sister's texts, and the list of who's helping is in your head.

This page doesn't ask you to understand or sort any of it. It asks who is involved, how to reach them, where each note is, and what date is on it.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Any row above with an empty box. Put a name next to each.

For example No phone number for the nurse who called on Thursday. My sister will play the voicemail again tonight.

How to use it

  • Write the date on each note or paper. For something you were told by phone, write the day of the call and who told you.
  • Don't copy out or summarize anything here. Say where it is and who has it.
  • Care notes are about Dad. Ask him before you collect them or pass them along, and if an office holds a record you need, ask that office what it requires before it can share it with you.
  • Bring this page to the next conversation about his care.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any note, record or instruction means, and it doesn't settle which version of events is right. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the person who wrote it.

Ready for the next step?

The names, numbers, notes and dates are on one page now, and you can see what's missing. The care interview puts them to use: it asks about Dad's situation area by area, checks what's been left out, and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.

Where this comes from

Keeping one list of contacts and noting where each item is kept follows AARP's Prepare to Care guide. Writing down the names and phone numbers of the people to call, and the dates of upcoming appointments, follows Medicare's discharge planning checklist. The rest comes from the Family Care Roadmap's working list for this step.
